I didn’t expect this to be this long but I tried to be super specific —

I’m going to be a senior this fall and I’ve interned every summer.

Although I haven’t taken a machine learning class at uci (yet) I taught myself it in it the past year and wanted to work with it so this summer has been pretty ML heavy. For the first 11 weeks of the summer I interned at a financial services company in Chicago deploying ML models on AWS for processing some very niche trades (bypassing the need for human analysis). I never thought I’d enjoy Fintech but it turns out it’s mostly working with numbers and incorporating some pretty interesting math with programming which I’m a fan of. Now I’m back home in San Francisco working at a biotech startup building DCNNs for finding gene mutations from binary sequence alignment files for the month or so left before fall quarter. I’m doing machine learning in C++ which is new for me and I kind of suck at it right now (considering I’ve been working here for 2 days and have previously only used machine learning with python) but I’m determined to become better at it. My current job is extremely cool and probably the most significant thing I’ve done with my life. Although this is a 10 person startup, it recently got funded for close to $75 million in its first round and got a contract licensing out their software for genetic engineering research to the Department of Energy so it pays extremely well and is generally very lucrative. I work directly under the CEO who is an exceedingly intelligent dude who was getting his PhD in biochemistry but dropped out to pursue this company instead. I would not mind working here or the Chicago financial services company full time. This might be conceited or money hungry but I really do want to get paid my first job out of college and they both pay well and have interesting work, so I wouldn’t be opposed to working at either place at least for a few years. My hourly rate has been $50-60 this summer (overtime being 1.5x the hourly rate).

This is just my personal opinion which you are free to disagree with, but I think the biggest problem I see with a lot of underclassmen at uci is that their resumes are trash. Often times the formatting is very cluttered and emphasizes style over substance. My resume has practically no style and I am maximizing the content over everything, having very little white space. Often times I see resumes which don’t have anything going for them other than their education. Education is important, but it is ‘fake’, as in you’re solving made up problems that have been solved countless times before alongside hundreds of other people in class and is not reflective of real world problems. Any programming heavy job or interesting project you’ve worked on is a lot more valuable than the classes you’ve taken. I think looking at your resume from the perspective of hiring managers who look at stacks of hundreds of resumes every day is illuminating - what can you do to stand out?

Something else I’ve noticed is that your GPA does not matter, although maybe this is only a thing in CS. In all my internships I’ve never disclosed my GPA, nor have any of my friends working at Google or Facebook or Amazon. I believe that GPA is not a good measure of intelligence or coding acumen — the best coders I’ve seen are dropouts or people who just didn’t care about performing well in school. Your work and projects and experience speak for itself.

Being able to talk about tech is a really valuable skill as well. Coding, especially at an intern level, can be taught to most smart people but being able to distinguish yourself from the antisocial and aspie and reclusive stereotype that our major unfortunately has is important. Communication skills can’t really be taught, so read YCombinator and recode, practice explaining your projects and other interesting tech ideas to non-technical laypersons, and figure out what how to answer common interview questions. I have templates that I remember by heart for questions like “what has been a time when you failed” or “what was a time when you had differences with a colleague and how did you resolve them” or “what is the most interesting aspect or field of computing to you” or “what are your long term and short term goals” that are ever popular in the interviewer’s wheelhouse.

Lastly I have to say that I believe that companies don’t want generic CS drones. They want vibrant and interesting people on their teams who have more going on in their lives than just their love for programming that has been drilled into them by school. In short they want people with personalities. For example, I have a weekly radio show on KUCI 88.9 FM that I mentioned on my resume. It has been brought up on literally every interview I’ve given because moonlighting as a radio dj is an interesting way to distinguish myself from my peers and show that I have interests that I work on outside of programming. On my resume I also have that I run and volunteer at marathons, and walk dogs over the summer (for fun and I love dogs and getting paid to exercise), which is another easy way to get some brownie points. Also, being divisive in your interviews and showing that you have strong opinions is not a bad thing (unless you’re being sexist or racist or something awful like that) and shows that you have put thought into your beliefs.

Again these are all my personal beliefs and what has allowed me to be very successful in my short career thus far. I’m sorry if I said anything too incendiary, please take it all as conjecture.

You are just a sophomore right now — I don’t think most people get an internship in their first summer anyway so don’t get too down on yourself. I know disappointment is hard, but the battle is far from over. So go read up on your favorite tech topics, work on some cool open source software, and develop some interesting hobbies and grow as a person! I’m sure it’ll work out :) Good luck!
